newsitem.title: ALBANIA: OSCE envoy seeks Albania aid, ruling party unhappy.
newsitem.headline: OSCE envoy seeks Albania aid, ruling party unhappy.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky called for economic aid to underpin Albania's largely peaceful general election, but President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, headed for defeat, said it would challenge some results.

Vranitzky, who brokered a deal between Albania's squabbling political parties in March to hold the early election, had brief meetings with Berisha and interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino soon after arriving in Tirana on Tuesday.
The former Austrian chancellor said he was told by Berisha that he had accepted the verdict of the people which meant his Democratic Party would now be entering opposition.
But Vranitzky, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe mission with 450 observers, said the president gave no indication whether he would step down after five years in power.
"No, he did not mention it and I did not ask him," he said.
Diplomatic sources said Berisha look tired and glum during the meeting with Vranitzky.
The president admitted in a television address on Monday that the Democrats had lost the election and many Albanians interpreted the statement as a hint that he was stepping down.
As head of state, Berisha has to wait for parliament to be convened before he can offer his resignation.
Results declared in 25 of 115 districts run under majority rules confirmed the big swing to the Socialists. They won 13 seats, with two more going to their Social Democratic allies.
The Democrats captured three seats while the remaining go through to a run-off next Sunday because no candidate won the 50 percent required for victory in the first round.

Vranitzky said last Sunday's election was "a first step...towards reconstructing Albania", to be followed up by Western-backed moves to rebuild the economy and reform the judiciary and other institutions.
"It has to be made quite clear that once the elections are over...that everyone in the international community is not going to pack their suitcases and go home," Vranitzky said.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) all had a role in injecting new financial blood into the former communist state, he said.
Vranitzky said Interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino had told him a government was likely to be formed by the end of July.
The Democrats' Secretary General, Genc Pollo, said his party wanted a rerun of voting in more than 20 districts in southern Albania, which has been the centre of months of armed upheaval.
"We cannot accept the result in those areas," he told a news conference. "The courts will have to decide."
Pollo also said the vote, described by the OSCE as "adequate and acceptable", was no fairer than last year's election.
That vote was won by the Democrats but boycotted by the Socialists and dismissed as flawed by international observers.
Although few incidents were reported in the south, no one in the aftermath of the election's first round has yet suggested how to restore law and order there.
Armed gangs still control most of the south after months of unrest sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes.

Vranitzky and OSCE election certification officer Catherine Lalumiere were to leave Tirana on Tuesday evening for Copenhagen to brief the OSCE's chairman-in-office, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen.
Prime Minister Fino praised Vranitzky's role in staging an orderly vote, describing him as "the chief factor in solving the crisis and conducting free and democratic elections".
